### ADHD Weekly Planner

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/adhd-weekly-reset.html


Most planners fail adult ADHD brains for a boring reason: they're designed by and for people whose brains cooperate. The Weekly Reset flips the design — one page, one sitting, and a Sunday routine that takes about an hour.

#### Why Sunday evening works for ADHD planning

Monday-morning planning collides with the hardest executive-function moment of the week. Planning on Sunday, when the pressure is off, means decisions are already made when Monday shows up. The reset walks you through four moves:

1. **Brain dump** — everything spinning in your head, onto one page [(grab the free brain-dump template)](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/adhd-brain-dump-template.html).

2. **Decide** — pick the one thing that actually matters this week.

3. **Defer** — explicitly park everything else where Future You can find it.

4. **Set the first move** — one concrete action for Monday, so you start moving instead of deciding.

#### Who it's for

If you've abandoned four planner apps and a wall of sticky notes; if your to-do list is a guilt archive; if "just use a checklist" has never once worked — this was designed for exactly that brain.

#### Format

Printable PDF, print-at-home. Weekly page plus support sheets. Instant digital download — no shipping, no waiting.

#### FAQ

##### How do I reset my week with ADHD?

Run a short Sunday ritual: dump every task onto one page, cross off anything that survived being ignored, shrink the rest to five-minute first steps, and assign exactly one anchor task per day. Pre-plan the comeback for the day after you slip. Thirty minutes, once a week — see the full [ADHD weekly reset routine](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/printable-adhd-weekly-reset.html).

##### Why do weekly planners fail ADHD brains?

A weekly list front-loads every decision onto your lowest-energy day and has no recovery path after one missed day. The reset replaces the list with one anchor task per day and a written comeback plan, so a bad Tuesday doesn't cancel the week.

##### What is an ADHD weekly reset?

A short planning ritual done at the same time every week — usually Sunday evening — where you empty your head onto one page, choose a single priority, park the rest, and set one concrete first move for Monday. It replaces the long weekly to-do list that ADHD brains tend to abandon by Wednesday.

##### What should be on an ADHD weekly reset checklist?

Four moves: a brain dump of everything on your mind; a decide step choosing the single thing that matters most this week; a defer step parking everything else where future you can find it; and one concrete first action for Monday. One anchor task per day plus a written comeback plan complete the checklist.

##### How long does a weekly reset take?

About an hour, once a week, ideally Sunday evening. Most of the time goes to the brain dump and choosing the week's priority — and once it's a ritual, it runs on habit instead of willpower.

The printable [monthly habit tracker](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/monthly-habit-tracker.html)'s never-miss-twice rule is the daily tick under this system.

### Menopause Symptom Tracker

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/menopause-symptom-tracker.html


"How have your symptoms been?" is the worst question in menopause care — because the honest answer is a shrug. Memories of hot flashes compress into "a lot?", sleep trouble blurs, and appointment prep happens in the parking lot. This tracker replaces the shrug with 90 days of data.

#### What's inside

- **Daily log** — symptoms, severity, sleep, triggers suspected. Two minutes a day.

- **Trigger finder** — after a few weeks, patterns surface: caffeine, alcohol, stress, heat, cycle timing.

- **Doctor visit prep page** — a one-page summary you walk in with: frequency, severity, what changed, what you want to discuss.

#### Why 90 days

Perimenopause symptoms fluctuate on long cycles. A week's diary tells your doctor almost nothing; 90 days shows trends, frequency, and whether what you changed actually helped. It also turns "I feel crazy" into a chart — which helps the person holding it as much as the one reading it.

#### Format

Printable PDF, print-at-home. Instant download.

The same bring-the-log mechanic covers the whole household's medications — the printable [medication tracker](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/medication-tracker.html) is the human-side version.

##### What should I bring to a menopause appointment?

The tracker's own answer: your data, not a shrug. The doctor visit prep page is a one-page summary you walk in with: frequency, severity, what changed, and what you want to discuss.

##### How do I track menopause symptoms?

On the daily log: symptoms, severity, sleep and suspected triggers, about two minutes a day, run across 90 days instead of a single remembered week.

##### Why track menopause symptoms for 90 days?

Perimenopause symptoms fluctuate on long cycles. A week's diary tells your doctor almost nothing; 90 days shows trends, frequency, and whether what you changed actually helped. It also turns "I feel crazy" into a chart, which helps the person holding it as much as the one reading it.

##### Can a symptom tracker identify my triggers?

The trigger finder works after a few weeks of logging: patterns around caffeine, alcohol, stress, heat and cycle timing surface from your own data rather than guesswork.

##### How long does the daily log take?

About two minutes a day: check symptoms, mark severity, note sleep and any trigger you suspect.

### 12-Month Wedding Planning Checklist

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/wedding-planning-checklist.html


Every wedding checklist tells you *when* to book the caterer. Almost none tell you *what to say* when you call them — which is where budgets quietly die. This one includes exact vendor scripts.

#### The three parts

1. **12-month countdown** — month-by-month bookings and deadlines, so nothing lands the month of the wedding.

2. **Budget worksheet** — every deposit, balance and due date in one sheet, with the running total visible.

3. **Vendor scripts** — word-for-word questions for caterers, photographers, venues and florists: the ones about hidden fees, overtime rates, backup plans, and what happens if it rains.

#### Why scripts matter

Asking a photographer "what's your overtime rate?" before signing saves the argument after. Asking the venue "what's included in the service charge?" before the tasting saves four figures. The scripts take the awkwardness out of asking — you're just following the sheet.

#### Format

Printable PDF worksheets, print-at-home. Instant download.

##### What is in the Wedding Planning Master Checklist?

Three parts: the 12-month countdown with month-by-month bookings and deadlines; the budget worksheet holding every deposit, balance and due date in one sheet with the running total visible; and the vendor scripts, word-for-word questions covering hidden fees, overtime rates, backup plans and rain.

##### How far in advance should I plan my wedding?

The countdown runs on a 12-month timeline, with month-by-month bookings and deadlines so nothing lands in the month of the wedding.

##### How do I keep a wedding budget on track?

On the budget worksheet: every deposit, balance and due date in one sheet, with the running total visible, so the money sits on paper instead of in memory.

##### Why does the checklist include vendor scripts?

Because the questions nobody asks until later are where budgets quietly die. Asking a photographer about the overtime rate before signing, or the venue what's included in the service charge before the tasting, replaces the argument after. Following the sheet also takes the awkwardness out of asking.

### DTF File Checklist

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/dtf-preflight-checklist.html


Every DTF print shop knows the moment: the file looked fine on screen, the customer approved the mockup, and the print comes out fuzzy, translucent, or with whites gone transparent. That's a wasted film, a wasted press, and a reprint for free.

#### What actually goes wrong with DTF files

- **Transparent whites** — white at 0% opacity vanishes on film and the shirt shows through.

- **Fuzzy edges** — low-res art scaled up, or vector strokes too thin to hold powder.

- **Missing traps** — colors that butt against each other with a hairline gap that opens on press.

- **Wrong DPI or size** — the file prints at half the garment size, or softens at 3x.

#### How Preflight works

Affinity DTF Preflight is a V3 script for Affinity Designer/Publisher that scans the file and flags exactly those problems — before you burn film. It runs in seconds and pays for itself the first time it catches the print that would have been trash.

#### For

DTF print shops, garment decorators, and anyone who prints customer files and eats the cost when they're wrong. $14.90. One bad print prevented = paid.

[Get Affinity DTF Preflight (V3) — $14.90 →](https://cooneymartin.gumroad.com/l/affinity-dtf-preflight?utm_source=fixshelf-hub&utm_medium=site&utm_campaign=affinity-dtf-preflight)

### Halftone Effect for Affinity

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/halftone-effect-affinity.html


Retro halftone effects look great on screen and die on DTF film. Gradient halftones built with blur and blend modes fall apart when the file hits RIP software — dots merge, gradients band, and the print loses the whole effect.

#### Built for print, not for screen

Affinity Studio DTF Halftone generates real, print-safe halftone patterns — proper dot structures, correct angles, sizes that hold through powder and press. One click from your art to a print-ready halftone version.

#### Works with

Affinity Designer and Publisher (V3 scripts). Pairs well with [Preflight](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/dtf-preflight-checklist.html) — run the check, then apply the halftone — and [Texture Engine](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/grunge-texture-affinity.html) for the full distressed-retro look.

### Grunge Texture Effect for Affinity — Real Wear Without Hand Masking

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/grunge-texture-affinity.html


The hand-blended grunge routine: buy texture packs, set blend modes, mask, erase, undo, repeat — an hour per design, and it still looks like a texture pasted on top.

#### What the Texture Engine does differently

It wears the texture *into* the ink rather than layering it on top: distress maps from any texture, applied to your artwork as authentic print wear. The result reads like a vintage tee that's been washed fifty times, not a Photoshop filter.

#### For

Apparel designers and print shops doing distressed, vintage, or retro garments. Runs in Affinity (V3 script). Combine with [Halftone](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/halftone-effect-affinity.html) for the full vintage-print look.

[Get Affinity Texture Engine — $19.90, instant download →](https://cooneymartin.gumroad.com/l/affinity-texture-engine?utm_source=fixshelf-hub&utm_medium=site&utm_campaign=affinity-texture-engine)

### Printable Vegetable Garden Planner

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/vegetable-garden-planner.html


Most gardeners plant by memory and regret it by August — tomatoes where the beans should have rotated, a bed that sat empty all June, no record of what actually produced. This planner replaces memory with paper.

### Reactive Dog Training Plan

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/reactive-dog-roadmap.html


A reactive dog makes every walk a negotiation: the barking at other dogs, the lungeing, the dread of passing a fence line. Punishment makes it worse. This roadmap follows the force-free method professional trainers use — distance, threshold, reward — paced over six weeks.

#### What's inside

- **6-week plan** — week-by-week exercises from foundation skills to real-world walks.

- **Trigger log** — what set your dog off, at what distance, how they recovered. The log is where progress becomes visible.

- **Walk scripts** — exact routines for the moments that go wrong: another dog appears, a cyclist passes, the hallway is crowded.

#### Who it's for

Owners of dogs that bark and lunge on leash — the ones already called "that dog." Works alongside a trainer or standalone. Printable PDF, instant download.

##### Can you train a reactive dog at home?

Yes for mild-to-moderate reactivity: the core work is finding the distance where your dog can still think and rewarding calm there, then shrinking that distance gradually. Severe reactivity — biting, injuries, or no safe distance at all — needs a certified force-free trainer alongside any home plan. The roadmap includes the "when to call a trainer" checklist.

##### What causes leash reactivity in dogs?

Most commonly fear, frustration, or a learned history — the dog barks because it worked, or because the thing on the other end scared them. Reactivity is not dominance. Understanding which driver your dog has changes which exercise you start with, which is why the roadmap opens with a trigger log before any training plan.

##### How long does reactive dog training take?

Months of consistent, short sessions is the honest default — progress shows up as a bigger working distance, not a cured dog. A six-week plan builds the habit and the tracking; some dogs move faster and some need a trainer's help. Every walk is data, which is what the trigger log is for.

### Anxiety Grounding Cards

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/anxiety-grounding-toolkit.html


In a spike of anxiety, the advice "just breathe" is useless — the working mind that remembers techniques is exactly what's offline. The fix is having the steps already on paper, where you don't have to think of them.

#### What's inside

- **Grounding cards** — printable cards with 5-4-3-2-1, cold-water, counting and movement techniques; keep them where anxiety happens.

- **Panic plan** — one page: my early warning signs, my first move, my next three steps, who I contact. Written by you on a calm day, read on a bad one.

- **Nightly offload** — the page that catches tomorrow's worries tonight, so 11pm stops being planning hour.

#### Who it's for

Anyone managing anxiety day to day — as a companion to therapy or between sessions, not a replacement. Printable PDF, instant download.

##### What is the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique?

Name five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, and one you can taste. It works because panic recruits all of attention; giving each sense a job takes that attention back. Our toolkit includes it as a card you can keep in a wallet, so you don't have to remember the steps mid-panic.

##### Do grounding techniques actually work for anxiety?

They interrupt the spiral in the moment — they pull attention back to the present through the senses. They are a skill, not a cure: they work better with practice, and they don't replace care from a professional if anxiety is frequent or severe. Our cards exist for the moments when remembering the steps is the hard part.

##### What's in the Anxiety Grounding Toolkit?

Printable grounding cards (wallet-size, one technique per card), a panic plan page you fill in when you're calm so future-you doesn't have to think, and a nightly offload sheet. Instant digital download, print at home, use today.

### Overthinking Workbook Printable

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/overthinking-workbook.html


Overthinking doesn't feel like a problem while it's happening — it feels like being thorough. But two hours of second-guessing a decision you already made isn't analysis; it's a loop. This workbook gives the loop three exits.

#### What's inside

- **The Decision Filter** — a page that forces a decision through a few sharp questions and closes it, so it stops reopening at 1am.

- **The Worry Court** — put a worry on trial: what's the evidence, what actually happens next, what would you tell a friend with this exact worry?

- **The Replay Repair** — for the conversations you keep re-running. Extract the one lesson, write it down once, and file the replay for good.

#### Why paper works

Overthinking runs in your head because your head is where the loop lives. Writing the worry down forces it into a fixed form — and a fixed worry can be examined, answered and closed in a way a circling thought never is.

#### Format

Printable PDF, print-at-home. Instant download.

##### How do I stop overthinking at night?

Keep a pad on the nightstand and offload the loop in one line each — the thought, not the argument. Night overthinking feeds on having nowhere to put things; giving each worry a line on paper ends the rehearsal. The workbook's nightly offload page gives that pad a structure, so morning-you can sort what was real.

##### What is the difference between overthinking and problem-solving?

Problem-solving ends in a decision or an action; overthinking repeats without producing one. The test is simple: if you've circled the same thought three times with nothing new written down, you're looping, not solving. The workbook's decision filter is built to force that exit — two questions, then a choice you can act on.

##### What's inside the Overthinking Workbook?

Three printable tools: a decision filter for future-worry, a worry court page for testing a spiral's evidence, and a replay repair page for conversations that keep looping. Each is a fill-in sheet you can print and reuse. It's a digital download — buy, print, use the same day.

### Burnout Recovery Workbook Printable

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/burnout-recovery-workbook.html


Burnout advice tends to be "take a vacation" — which doesn't fix the structure that exhausted you. Recovery needs a diagnosis first: what exactly is draining the tank, and a climb back that doesn't rely on willpower you don't have.

#### What's inside

- **The Check** — a honest self-assessment of where you actually are: cynicism, exhaustion, efficacy. You can't recover from a level you won't name.

- **The Energy Audit** — one week of logging what gave energy and what drained it, across work, people, home and body. The drains are usually specific, and specific things can be changed.

- **The 6-Week Ladder** — one recovery rung a week: boundaries, sleep, delegation, recovery time that's actually scheduled — sequenced so each week is survivable.

#### Who it's for

Anyone running on fumes who can't just quit — employees, caregivers, founders, parents. It works alongside medical care, not instead of it. Printable PDF, instant download.

##### How long does burnout recovery take?

Weeks for lighter burnout, months for deep burnout — the honest range, and anyone promising days is selling something. The useful test is whether your energy survives a normal week, not whether you had one good day. The workbook's weekly check tracks exactly that, so you can see the trend instead of guessing.

##### Can you recover from burnout without quitting your job?

Often yes, but not by resting harder inside the same load — something structural has to change: boundaries, task volume, or support. Recovery is subtraction first. The workbook's energy audit shows you where the drain actually is, and its ladder rebuilds capacity in steps that survive a bad week at the same job.

##### What is the first step to recover from burnout?

A check, not a change. Before adding routines or quitting anything, spend one week recording where energy goes and what returns any. Most people find one or two drains they can cut immediately. The workbook opens with exactly that check, then builds the 6-week ladder on what it finds.

Rebuild weeks need small wins — the printable [monthly habit tracker](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/monthly-habit-tracker.html) is where the daily tick lives.

### Wedding Speech Builder Printable

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/wedding-speech-builder.html


Every wrecked wedding speech failed the same three ways: too long, too drunk, or too inside-jokey. The Wedding Speech Builder prevents all three with prompt worksheets, a hard timer and a banned list — for the best man, the maid of honor, and the couple themselves.

#### What's inside

- **Prompt worksheets per role** — separate pages for best man, maid of honor and the couple, each with the prompts that build a speech structurally instead of blank-page panic.

- **The hard timer** — a length budget with a word count per section, because the speech that "felt short while writing it" is never short at the microphone.

- **The banned list** — the ex stories, the arrests, the finance jokes and every other crowd-tested disaster category, ruled out before they reach the draft.

#### Why worksheets and not tips

Speech advice is everywhere and it doesn't write the speech. The worksheets do: each prompt pulls one true story or one honest quality onto paper, the timer cuts it to deliverable length, and the banned list catches the joke that plays great in a group chat and dies in a marquee. Printable PDF, instant download.

##### How long should a wedding speech be?

Three to five minutes is the range guests forgive — roughly 400 to 650 words spoken. The builder's hard timer converts that to a per-section word budget, so the speech is short by construction rather than by hope. Longer speeches are remembered, but for the wrong reason.

##### What should a best man speech include?

A short introduction and how you know the groom, one or two genuinely funny but safe stories, a sincere word about the couple's relationship, and a toast to end on. The best man worksheet walks exactly that arc with prompts per section — and the banned list marks the ex-partner and arrest-story territory before you're tempted.

##### What should the maid of honor say in her speech?

Typically: your relationship to the bride, one story that shows who she was before this wedding, what you've watched the partnership do to her, and a warm close with the toast. The maid of honor worksheet prompts each part separately, so the speech builds instead of spiralling.

##### When should you start planning for Christmas?

Six weeks out is the practical answer: early enough that gifts arrive without rush fees and the food budget spreads across normal shops, late enough that the plan still feels real. Decide the total first, then split it per person before a single gift is bought — and write every purchase down as it happens. The gift tracker's budget column does exactly this: a known total, a per-person allocation, and a running record so December 24th never surprises the January statement.

### Debt Payoff Tracker Printable

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/debt-payoff-tracker.html


Paying off debt fails quietly, not dramatically: payments go out, the balances drift down, and there's no visible progress to keep the motivation fed. This tracker puts the whole payoff on paper — the plan, the log, and the date.

#### What's inside

- **Both plans, side by side** — the avalanche (highest interest first, cheapest overall) and the snowball (smallest balance first, fastest wins), laid out so you can pick with your own numbers.

- **The 12-month log** — every debt, every payment, every balance, one row per month, so progress is a filled-in page instead of a feeling.

- **The debt-free date** — computed from your actual plan and updated as you log payments, because a visible finish line changes how long people last.

#### Avalanche or snowball?

On pure maths, avalanche wins — kill the highest interest rate and every dollar works harder. On human maths, snowball wins more often — the early killed balances are the motivation that keeps the plan alive at month four. The tracker lays both out with your real numbers so the choice is yours and visible. Printable PDF, instant download.

The payoff plan sits inside a wider money lane: the [monthly money reset](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/monthly-money-reset.html) is the budget side that frees up the spare dollars a payoff plan needs, and the [tax prep checklist](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/tax-prep-checklist.html) keeps next April's return from undoing this year's progress.

##### What is the debt snowball method?

Listing every debt by balance, paying minimums on all of them, and throwing every spare dollar at the smallest balance until it's gone — then rolling that payment into the next smallest. The wins come fast and early, which is why it works for motivation even though the avalanche method is cheaper on interest.

##### How do you track debt payoff progress?

One row per debt per month: balance, payment, remaining. The point is visibility — a filled-in log shows the trend the bank app hides, and the debt-free date printed at the top of the page moves closer every time a payment lands. Progress you can see is progress you keep making.

##### Is it better to pay off small debts or high interest first?

High interest first saves the most money; small balances first keeps more people in the game. The tracker's side-by-side plan pages let you run your own debts both ways and see the difference — then commit to the one you'll actually still be following at month six.

Every dollar the envelope ladder catches is a payment this tracker can route — see the printable [savings challenge pack](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/savings-challenge-pack.html) and the daily [expense tracker](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/expense-tracker.html).

### Emergency Binder Printable

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/emergency-binder.html


When something goes wrong, the information your family needs is scattered — insurance policies in an email account, account numbers in one partner's password manager, and the wishes nobody wrote down. This binder gathers all of it into one findable place.

#### What's inside

- **Documents** — what each document is, where the original lives, and who needs a copy: IDs, policies, deeds, medical records.

- **Accounts** — the full financial picture on one page per person: what exists, who owns it, how it's accessed.

- **Wishes** — the section most families never write: what you'd want done, who decides what, and the conversations this page spares everyone.

#### The point of paper

In a crisis, nobody wants to learn a password manager or search an inbox. A binder on a known shelf works for whoever needs it — including the family member who isn't the family's accountant. Printable PDF, instant download.

##### What should be in a family emergency binder?

Eight sections cover it: identities and key documents, insurance policies, financial accounts, property records, pet care instructions, medical basics, end-of-life wishes, and a first-72-hours one-pager. The sections almost everyone forgets are passwords and digital accounts, and telling someone where the binder lives. The printable binder includes all sections as fill-in pages.

##### Where should you keep an emergency binder?

One obvious physical location — a specific shelf or safe the household knows — plus one backup copy stored separately, such as at a relative's home. Then tell at least one trusted person outside the household where it is; a binder nobody can find helps nobody. Update it once a year or after any big life change.

##### Is a paper or digital emergency binder better?

Both, on purpose. Paper works during a power outage and is instantly grab-and-go; a digital copy survives fire and flood. The practical setup is a paper binder as the master, plus one encrypted digital backup. Never store the binder's contents online unencrypted, and never publish your own details.

What the medication is, who takes it, a daily check-off for the week, and a refill tracker so you know when a supply runs low. Bring the filled log to appointments instead of reconstructing it from memory.

## Guides

### Salary Negotiation Script

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/salary-negotiation-script-guide.html


Last updated: November 12, 2026

Most salary advice is about confidence. But on the actual call — offer on the table, a pause getting longer — confidence doesn't say the sentence. A script does. Below are the sentences for the three moments that decide money: the ask, the email version, and the pushback. Adapt the bracketed fills; keep the structure.

#### The one rule before any script

Get the number first — and avoid naming the first number when you can. Whoever names a number first anchors the range, and every counter happens inside that anchor. Common practice, not law: sometimes the recruiter simply won't move without one. If you're forced to name a number, name a researched range whose *bottom* is a salary you'd actually accept — never a single bare figure, and never a range you'd turn down.

#### The offer-call script

When the number lands, don't respond to it live. The pause is the whole move:

1. Thank them genuinely: *"Thank you — I'm really pleased about this offer, and I'm excited about the role."*

2. Then the sentence that buys you a day: *"Could I take a day or two to review the full package? I'd like to give it proper consideration."* Almost nobody says no to this, and it removes every pressure to negotiate cold.

3. When you call back, the ask itself: *"I'm excited about the team and the work. Based on my research for this role and market in [city], and what I bring — [your two or three strongest wins] — I was expecting a base salary closer to [fill]. Is there flexibility?"*

Then stop talking. The silence after "Is there flexibility?" is where raises live. The first person to fill it usually concedes something.

#### The email version

If the offer arrived in writing, reply in writing — it's calmer and it creates a record:

*"Hi [name], thank you again for the offer — I'm genuinely excited about joining [team]. Before I accept, I'd like to discuss the base salary. Based on my research for this role in [location] and my experience in [your strongest relevant win], I was expecting a base in the range of [fill]. Is there flexibility on the base? Happy to jump on a call — I can be flexible on timing. Thanks again for the offer, and for considering this."*

Notice what the email does: enthusiasm stated before the ask, one reason (research + one win, not five), one number-range question, and gratitude at the end. Nothing else belongs in it.

#### The pushback replies

This is the section most guides skip, and it's where negotiations actually end:

**"The budget for this role is fixed."** — *"I understand budgets are set. If the base can't move, is there flexibility on [signing bonus / an earlier review at six months / additional leave / remote days]?"* You accept their frame and move to a lever they control.

**"We'll revisit your salary in six months."** — *"I appreciate that. Could we put the review in writing, with the criteria we'd both look at? That way we're working from the same page in six months."* A vague promise converts to a written criterion, or it reveals itself as a brush-off.

**"Another candidate was stronger / we have someone cheaper."** — *"I understand. Given you've chosen to make me this offer, I assume you believe I'll deliver — my ask is based on the value of that delivery, not the other candidate's rate. If the number can't work for both of us, I respect that."* Calm, and it puts the decision back where it belongs.

#### The promotion variant

Internal asks change in one way: your value is documented and known, so the research argument matters less than the record. Bring the wins list — the projects, the scope you took on, the coverage during vacancies — and anchor to the market rate for the *new* role, not a percentage off your current one. The conversation opens: *"I'd like to talk about the [new role] and the compensation that comes with it. Here's the scope I've already been carrying..."*

#### The full scripts pack

These scripts are the core of the printable [Salary Negotiation Scripts pack](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/salary-negotiation-scripts.html) — which adds the research-stack builder and the wins list worksheet, so the numbers and evidence behind the scripts are prepared before the call too. If you're still pre-offer, the [career change interview workbook](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/career-change-interview-workbook.html) covers the conversation one stage earlier.

##### What do you say when negotiating salary?

One sentence carries the ask: "Based on my research for this role and what I bring — [your strongest wins] — I was expecting a base salary closer to [number]. Is there flexibility?" Everything before it builds goodwill; everything after it is silence.

##### How do you negotiate salary over email?

Reply in writing with four parts: genuine enthusiasm for the role, the ask with one researched range, one supporting win, and thanks. Keep it under 150 words — the email's job is to book the conversation, not to have it.

##### What if they say the salary is not negotiable?

Accept the frame and switch levers: signing bonus, an earlier salary review with written criteria, extra leave, remote days, a title adjustment. If nothing moves, you've learned how the company treats its word before you've joined it — that is also useful information.

##### Should you accept the first job offer?

Ask once, politely — that's the whole rule. In ordinary experience, one courteous negotiation rarely costs an offer; employers expect it. What costs offers is how the asking is done: demanding, ultimatums, or negotiating after you've accepted. Ask once, kindly, then decide with the answer you get.

[See The Salary Negotiation Scripts — every variant, printable →](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/salary-negotiation-scripts.html?utm_source=fixshelf-hub&utm_medium=guide&utm_campaign=salary-negotiation-script-guide)

### Printable ADHD Weekly Reset

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/printable-adhd-weekly-reset.html


Last updated: November 12, 2026

The pattern is familiar: big plans on Sunday, abandoned by Wednesday, guilt spiral by Friday. It's not a discipline problem. A weekly to-do list is one giant front-loaded task, and a brain that manages executive function differently runs out of fuel deciding instead of doing. The fix isn't a better plan — it's a **reset**: a short ritual that shrinks the week down to something a Tuesday brain can still hold.

#### Why weekly checklists fail ADHD brains

**They front-load everything.** A 20-item weekly list asks you to make twenty decisions at once on your lowest-executive-function day. The list itself becomes the biggest task of the week — so it's the first thing you avoid.

**They have no comeback path.** Miss one day and the list is already "wrong," so the brain files the whole week as failed. A plan without a built-in recovery move turns one missed Monday into a lost week.

**They're plans, not rituals.** Plans depend on remembering and choosing every time. Rituals are the same short sequence every week, so by week three it runs on autopilot instead of willpower.

#### The 30-minute Sunday reset, step by step

Follow it as-is — it works without buying anything:

1. **Brain dump everything.** Every task, worry and "should" spinning in your head, onto one page. Ten minutes, no filtering.

2. **Cross off anything that survives being ignored.** Look at the dump and strike whatever sat there last week without the world ending. Usually a third of the list goes.

3. **Shrink each task to its 5-minute door.** Not "clean the kitchen" — "put the dishes in the rack." Not "do the taxes" — "find last year's return." The door is the part you walk through; momentum handles the rest.

4. **Assign one anchor task per day.** One. Not a list — a single thing that, done, makes the day count. Everything else is bonus.

5. **Pre-plan the comeback.** Write it now, while you're calm: "When I miss Monday, Tuesday starts with ___." A prepared recovery means one missed day stays one day.

6. **Park next week's guilt on one page.** Whatever you're not doing this week goes on a "later" page — deliberately, so it stops orbiting your head.

#### An example week (one anchor per day)

A realistic example — yours will differ:

| Day | Anchor task |
|---|---|
| Monday | Send the overdue email (door: open the draft) |
| Tuesday | Book the dentist (door: find the number) |
| Wednesday | Laundry start-to-done (door: move clothes to washer) |
| Thursday | Thirty minutes on the tax folder (door: open it) |
| Friday | Groceries for the week (door: write the five dinners) |
| Saturday | Free day — one catch-up item max, only if it's easy |
| Sunday | The reset itself (30 minutes) |

#### The printable version

The ADHD Weekly Reset printable is this routine made into pages: a Sunday reset sheet, an anchor-per-day spread, a task-shrinkage worksheet and the comeback page — print it, pin it, run the ritual. Two minutes of setup a week.

#### FAQ

##### How do I reset my week with ADHD?

Run a short Sunday ritual: dump every task onto one page, cross off anything that survived being ignored, shrink the rest to five-minute first steps, and assign exactly one anchor task per day. Pre-plan what you'll do the day after you slip. Thirty minutes, once a week.

##### What is an ADHD weekly reset?

A weekly planning routine redesigned for ADHD brains: instead of one big list, it produces one anchor task per day, pre-shrunk tasks, and a written comeback plan. The reset happens on Sunday when pressure is low, so Monday starts moving instead of deciding.

##### Why do ADHD to-do lists stop working after a few days?

A weekly list front-loads every decision onto your lowest-energy day and has no recovery path — one missed day makes the whole list feel "wrong." Shrinking tasks to five-minute doors and picking one anchor per day keeps the list small enough to survive a bad Tuesday.

##### What time should I do a weekly reset?

Sunday evening works for most people: the week's pressure is off, so planning costs less executive function than it does on Monday morning. Pick a slot you can repeat — same time every week matters more than which time you pick.

**Want it on paper?** Four of these pages exist as a free printable PDF — [download the free ADHD sampler (no email required)](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/free-adhd-printable-sampler.html).

[See The ADHD Weekly Reset printable →](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/adhd-weekly-reset.html?utm_source=fixshelf-hub&utm_medium=guide&utm_campaign=printable-adhd-weekly-reset)

### Wedding Day Timeline Template

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/wedding-day-timeline-template.html


Last updated: November 12, 2026

Pick your ceremony time below, copy the table, and adjust three variables: photo time, travel between sites, and sunset. These are workable defaults built to survive a 20-minute delay — not rigid schedules.

#### What time should you start getting ready?

For most weddings, hair and makeup start **3–4 hours before the ceremony for the couple**, and the wedding party joins about 90 minutes in. The buffer isn't beauty time — it absorbs the delayed makeup artist, the missing groomsman and the "just one more photo" that always happens.

**Assumptions:** ceremony and reception at one venue, couple on-site, roughly 4 bridesmaids and 4 groomsmen. Moving between sites? Add about 30 minutes per move, plus the buffer below. Rule of thumb, not a law — your vendors' quoted times override this table.

#### Timeline for a 2pm ceremony

| Time | Who | What |
|---|---|---|
| 9:00 am | Couple | Hair & makeup begins |
| 10:30 am | Wedding party | Party hair & makeup, breakfast within reach |
| 11:30 am | Couple | Dress/suit on, detail photos (rings, invitations) |
| 12:30 pm | Everyone | First look + wedding party photos |
| 1:00 pm | Guests | Guest arrival, ushers seated |
| 1:30 pm | Couple hidden | Touch-ups, water, five quiet minutes |
| 2:00 pm | All | Ceremony (~30 min) |
| 2:45 pm | All | Cocktail hour; couple does family formals |
| 3:45 pm | Couple | Golden-hour couple photos |
| 4:30 pm | All | Reception entrance, dinner service |
| 6:30 pm | All | Toasts, cake cutting |
| 8:00 pm | All | First dance, open floor |
| 10:00 pm | All | Last dance, send-off |

********

#### Timeline for a 3pm ceremony

Same structure, shifted an hour — and add a real lunch: an afternoon ceremony means nobody has eaten since breakfast, so feed the wedding party at 11:30.

| Time | Who | What |
|---|---|---|
| 10:00 am | Couple | Hair & makeup begins |
| 11:30 am | Wedding party | Party hair & makeup + lunch |
| 12:30 pm | Couple | Dress/suit on, detail photos |
| 1:30 pm | Everyone | First look + wedding party photos |
| 2:00 pm | Guests | Guest arrival |
| 2:30 pm | Couple hidden | Touch-ups, water, quiet five |
| 3:00 pm | All | Ceremony (~30 min) |
| 3:45 pm | All | Cocktail hour; family formals |
| 4:45 pm | Couple | Couple photos (sunset usually ~5–6pm — check your date) |
| 5:30 pm | All | Reception entrance, dinner |
| 7:30 pm | All | Toasts, cake cutting |
| 9:00 pm | All | First dance, open floor |
| 11:00 pm | All | Last dance, send-off |

********

#### Timeline for a 4pm ceremony

The evening version. Sunset lands mid-reception for much of the year — so couple photos move to cocktail hour, and the buffer shrinks: evening ceremonies eat their slack because dinner can't slide without pushing everything past venue cutoff.

| Time | Who | What |
|---|---|---|
| 11:00 am | Couple | Hair & makeup begins |
| 12:30 pm | Wedding party | Party hair & makeup + late lunch |
| 1:30 pm | Couple | Dress/suit on, detail photos |
| 2:15 pm | Everyone | First look + wedding party photos |
| 3:00 pm | Guests | Guest arrival |
| 3:30 pm | Couple hidden | Touch-ups, water, quiet five |
| 4:00 pm | All | Ceremony (~30 min) |
| 4:45 pm | All | Cocktail hour + family formals |
| 5:15 pm | Couple | Couple photos — sunset, then straight to reception |
| 6:00 pm | All | Reception entrance, dinner |
| 8:00 pm | All | Toasts, cake cutting, first dance |
| 9:00 pm | All | Open floor |
| 11:30 pm | All | Last dance, send-off |

********

#### The five things that break a wedding timeline

**Photography overruns.** Family formals balloon when the list isn't fixed in advance. Fix: hand your photographer a named list — 10 combos, not 25 — and a hard stop time.

**Vendor load-in.** The florist, DJ and caterer all arrive in the same hour. Fix: staggered load-in windows in the vendor sheet, and someone assigned to open the door.

**Bridal-party size.** Each extra person adds real minutes to hair, makeup and photos. Fix: scale the "start getting ready" time by party size, not by hope.

**Travel between sites.** Ceremony church, photos park, reception hall — each move costs 30 minutes plus rounding-up-the-party time. Fix: one venue, or one bus.

**"Just one more family photo."** Not a joke — it's the most common 20-minute leak in a reception. Fix: a designated family-photo wrangler with the list, who isn't you.

#### Make it yours

The Day-of Timeline Builder turns one of these skeletons into your schedule, with buffer rules, vendor distribution list and the who-gets-it list built in.

#### FAQ

##### What time should a wedding day start getting ready?

Start hair and makeup 3–4 hours before the ceremony for the couple, with the wedding party joining about 90 minutes in. The point of the early start is buffer for delays, not extra mirror time — the schedule that survives is the one with slack built in before the ceremony, not after.

##### What is a good wedding day timeline for a 4pm ceremony?

Workable default: hair and makeup at 11am, dress on 1:30pm, first look 2:15pm, guests at 3pm, ceremony at 4pm, cocktail hour 4:45pm with couple photos at sunset, dinner at 6pm, toasts at 8pm, last dance 11:30pm. Adjust for party size and travel.

##### How long should you allow for wedding photos?

A workable default: 45–60 minutes for family formals during cocktail hour and 20–30 minutes for couple photos, ideally at golden hour. Budget the time in the timeline itself — photos that "just happen" between events are the ones that overrun.

##### How much buffer time does a wedding timeline need?

Plan for one 20–30 minute buffer before the ceremony and at least one mid-reception buffer, placed where a delay does the least damage. If the day has no slack anywhere, the first late vendor pushes dinner, toasts and the venue cutoff all at once.

### Menopause Symptom Tracker Printable

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/menopause-symptom-tracker-printable.html


Last updated: November 12, 2026

"How have your symptoms been?" is the hardest question in menopause care, because the honest answer is usually a shrug. Months of hot flashes compress into "a lot?", sleep trouble blurs together, and the appointment happens before you've found the words. The fix is unglamorous: track for 90 days, and walk in with evidence instead of a shrug. One line first — this page helps you record and communicate symptoms; it doesn't diagnose anything or replace medical advice.

#### What symptoms are worth tracking

- **Hot flashes** — how many per day, and how severe (1–10).

- **Night sweats** — nights per week you wake soaked.

- **Sleep** — time to fall asleep, night wakes, how rested you feel (1–10).

- **Mood** — anxiety, irritability, low days; a one-word day label is enough.

- **Brain fog** — the days you couldn't find words or lost a thread mid-sentence.

- **Cycles** — start date, length, heaviness; perimenopause is often defined by the change in these.

- **Suspected triggers** — coffee, alcohol, stress, heat, poor sleep — noted alongside, not judged yet.

#### How to track so a doctor can use the data

Four fields per day, two minutes: **symptom, severity 1–10, possible trigger, date**. That's the whole method. The weekly summary is where patterns surface — "hot flashes peaked the week I restarted coffee" is a sentence your doctor can act on; "it's been rough lately" is not.

Perimenopause symptoms fluctuate on long cycles, which is why the 90-day window matters: a bad week looks like a trend, a good week looks like recovery, and only a quarter of data shows the real pattern underneath both.

#### The 90-day printable tracker

The Menopause Symptom Tracker printable is this method made usable: a daily log, a trigger finder that surfaces patterns after a few weeks, and a one-page doctor visit summary you fill in from the data instead of from memory.

#### Bringing your tracker to the appointment

Highlight three things the night before: your **worst symptom** (with frequency and severity), your **biggest change** since last visit, and the **one question** you most want answered. Hand over the summary page rather than reciting from memory — the doctor reads faster than you talk, and the page becomes part of your record.

#### Printable tracker or app?

Stated criteria: convenience, visibility, and handover. Apps win convenience — the phone is always with you. Printables win the other two: the log on the fridge is visible daily (apps hide in folders), and handing a doctor a printed page beats handing them your phone. Many people use both; the printable is the one that reaches the appointment.

#### FAQ

##### What is the best way to track menopause symptoms?

A daily log with four fields — symptom, severity 1–10, possible trigger, date — plus a weekly summary. Ninety days of that shows frequency, severity and patterns that weekly memory can't. The output that matters is a one-page summary you can hand your doctor at the appointment.

##### How do I track perimenopause symptoms for my doctor?

Record each symptom's frequency and severity with dates, keep a simple cycle log, and bring a one-page written summary to the appointment. Doctors act on frequency, severity and change-over-time — the three things memory is worst at reconstructing.

##### Is there a free menopause symptom tracker?

The method on this page is free to use with any notebook: symptom, severity, trigger, date, daily. The 90-day printable adds a structured daily log, a trigger finder and the doctor-visit summary page — the parts that are tedious to build yourself.

##### What symptoms should I track during perimenopause?

Hot flashes, night sweats, sleep quality, mood changes, brain fog, and your cycle dates and heaviness — plus suspected triggers like caffeine, alcohol and stress. Tracking all of them daily at low effort beats tracking one perfectly.

### Puppy Training Schedule by Age

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/puppy-training-schedule-by-age.html


Last updated: November 12, 2026

A new 8-week-old puppy arrives and the first question is not "what tricks should we teach" — it's "what is our day even supposed to look like?" Here's the schedule by age: one rhythm per life stage, feeding to potty to naps to short training slots. Everything below is a labeled rule of thumb to adjust to your puppy, not a vet prescription.

#### What changes at each age

| Age | Feeds/day | Sleep (rule of thumb) | Potty when awake | Training focus |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8–10 weeks | 3–4 | 18–20 hrs/day | every 1–2 hrs | Name, potty spot, crate = safe |
| 3 months | 3 | 15–18 hrs/day | every 2–3 hrs | Sit/come, socialization window |
| 4–6 months | 2–3 | 14–16 hrs/day | every 3–4 hrs | Loose leash, "regression is normal" |
| 6–12 months | 2 | 12–16 hrs/day | longer holds | Consolidation, adolescence management |

#### 8–10 weeks: the everything-is-new stage

The day is a loop: **wake → potty outside → feed → play 10 minutes → potty again → nap.** Puppies this age sleep most of the day, and an overtired puppy bites harder — enforced naps aren't spoiling, they're management. Potty breaks every 1–2 hours awake, always after eating, playing or waking. Training is minutes a day: their name, the potty spot, and the crate as the best place in the house.

#### 3 months: the socialization window

Feeds drop to three, stretches between potty breaks lengthen, and the crate rhythm sets: wake, potty, train, play, nap, repeat. This stage has one job vets and trainers agree on — **gentle, positive exposure to new people, surfaces, sounds and handling** while the window is wide open. Keep sessions two to five minutes.

#### 4–6 months: adolescence starts

Feeds settle to two or three, naps consolidate, and the leash walk becomes a daily thing — loose-leash practice starts now, before pulling is a habit. The headline of this stage: **training regression is normal.** The puppy that "had" sit suddenly doesn't. That's adolescence, not failure — go back to short sessions and high-value rewards without panicking.

#### 6–12 months: consolidation and the teenage months

Two feeds, adult sleep patterns, and bladder capacity that finally holds through the night for most puppies. Adolescence peaks somewhere in this window — recall gets selective, and the answer is more practice in boring places, not longer leash. By twelve months the daily rhythm you built is simply "the routine," and the year's logs (vaccines, weights, milestones) are the record every future vet visit wants.

#### The printable version

The Puppy's First Year Planner turns each stage into a wall chart: potty and accident logs, month-by-month milestone checklists, and vet logs for vaccines and weigh-ins. If reactivity shows up later, it pairs with the [New Puppy Bundle](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/new-puppy-bundle.html).

#### FAQ

##### What is a good schedule for an 8-week-old puppy?

A workable default loop: wake → potty → feed → 10 minutes of play → potty → nap, repeating all day with a final potty before bed. Expect 3–4 feeds, naps most of the day, and potty breaks every 1–2 hours while awake. Adjust to your puppy — the loop matters more than the exact times.

##### How long can a puppy hold its bladder?

The common rule of thumb is roughly one hour per month of age, plus one — a 3-month-old might hold it about four hours at most. Start lower and succeed more: an accident-free record builds the habit faster than testing the maximum.

##### How much do puppies sleep?

A lot: 18–20 hours a day at 8–10 weeks, settling toward 12–16 hours by adolescence. Overtired puppies bite and melt down more, so scheduled naps in the crate help behavior as much as rest. If your puppy is a terror at 7pm, the cause is usually missing naps, not attitude.

##### When should puppies start training?

The day they come home. Eight-week-old puppies learn name recognition, potty spot and crate association immediately — sessions of one to three minutes, many times a day. Formal obedience classes can start once the vet confirms vaccine timing; the foundation starts now, free.

[Track the whole year with The Puppy's First Year Planner →](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/puppy-first-year-planner.html?utm_source=fixshelf-hub&utm_medium=guide&utm_campaign=puppy-training-schedule-by-age)

### Wedding Planning Checklist Printable

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/wedding-planning-checklist-printable.html


Last updated: November 12, 2026

Nine to twelve months out, the advice online adds up to one 300-item monster list — which is exactly the kind of list nobody works through. This version is scoped differently: **each month owns a handful of decisions**, and the checklist tells you what to stop thinking about until its month arrives. Start at your month, ignore everything before it.

#### How to use this checklist

Find your months-out number, read only that block, do the handful of things in it, and close the tab. The whole trick to non-overwhelming wedding planning is refusing to think about months that aren't yours yet. Everything below is a convention, not a rule — your venue's and vendors' timelines override this.

#### 12 months out → 6 months out

- **Month 12–10:** venue and date locked (they gate everything), rough budget with a running total, guest count draft, engagement photos if you want them.

- **Month 9–8:** photographer, caterer, and officiant booked; save-the-dates addressed. Book vendors with question scripts, not vibes — see the [Vendor Question Scripts](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/vendor-question-scripts.html).

- **Month 7–6:** dress bought (alterations eat months), registry started, hotel blocks reserved, wedding party formally asked.

#### 6 months out → 3 months out

- **Month 5:** invitations ordered, flowers and cake booked, menu tasting.

- **Month 4:** dress fitting one, suit sorted, ceremony readings chosen, day-of transportation confirmed.

- **Month 3:** invitations mailed, final dress fitting scheduled, marriage license paperwork looked up (some counties have waiting periods).

#### Final 3 months

- **Month 2:** RSVPs chased (yes, the silent 20%), seating chart drafted, vendor payments scheduled against payday, song list with the DJ/band.

- **Month 1:** final fittings, vendor confirmations in writing, and — the month's real job — the [day-of timeline](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/wedding-day-timeline-template.html) built and sent to every vendor and the wedding party.

#### The last 2 weeks

Confirmations only: reconfirm arrival times with every vendor, pack the emergency bag (sewing kit, snacks, flats, chargers, cash for tips), hand a trusted person the vendor day-of contact list, and stop adding tasks. The plan is done; the job now is showing up.

#### What the printable adds

The Wedding Planning Master Checklist puts all twelve months on printable sheets plus the two parts most checklists skip: the budget worksheet with every deposit and due date visible, and the vendor scripts.

#### FAQ

##### When should you start planning a wedding?

Twelve months out is comfortable; nine is workable if you move fast on the venue. Book the venue and date first because they decide the guest count, the budget shape and every vendor's availability — everything else chains off that decision.

##### What are the most important things to book first for a wedding?

Venue and date, then photographer, then caterer. The venue gates everything — capacity, date, budget. Photographers and good caterers book single dates and disappear a year out. Everything else has more supply and can be chosen later.

##### How far in advance should you send wedding invitations?

By convention: save-the-dates around six months out, formal invitations about eight weeks before, with RSVPs due a month out so the final count reaches caterers in time. Destination weddings run earlier. These are workable defaults, not rules.

##### What should a wedding budget include that people forget?

Vendor tips, dress alterations, invitation postage, day-of snacks for the wedding party, the marriage license fee, overtime rates, cake-cutting and corkage fees, and buffers for weather plans. The forgotten lines are rarely big — they're just never on the first list.

### Vegetable Garden Planner Printable

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/vegetable-garden-planner-printable.html


Last updated: November 12, 2026

Most garden "planning" is a planting list — and planting lists fail by July, because a list doesn't say what goes where, when it goes in, or what actually produced last year. A garden plan that gets used has three parts: a map, a calendar, and a log. Here's how each one works on paper.

#### The three parts of a garden plan that gets used

A list tells you what to buy. A **map** tells you what goes where — and prevents planting the shade-lover behind the six-foot tomatoes. A **calendar** tells you when, anchored to your frost dates. The **log** is the part everyone skips and the part that compounds: it's the reason year three is better than year one. Lists alone fail because they answer none of the three questions that actually decide a season.

#### Mapping your beds

Draw each bed to scale on a gridded page — graph paper is fine. Three passes:

1. **Sun** — note which edges get blasted by afternoon light and which stay shaded; this decides the layout more than anything else.

2. **Spacing** — place crops by their real spacing (the seed packet's, not the wishful one), tall crops on the north edge so they don't shade everything else.

3. **Paths** — mark where you'll actually walk. A bed you can't reach into without stepping in it is a bed you'll stop weeding by June.

#### The planting calendar

Everything keys off one number you write at the top of the page: **your last frost date**. Frost dates are local — look yours up for your own ZIP code and write it on the calendar page. Then work backwards: tomatoes started indoors about 6–8 weeks before it, peas and greens sown well before it, heat-lovers like basil long after. The calendar's job is turning "when do I plant X?" into arithmetic you only do once.

#### What to log during the season

Four lines per crop is a complete log: what you planted and when, what produced (and roughly how much, so "the tomatoes did great" becomes "Roma outgrew Cherry"), what got eaten or diseased, and one honest verdict — plant again, change something, or skip next year. The log is the page that makes next year's map and calendar better instead of starting over.

#### The printable planner

The Vegetable Garden Planner is this loop on paper: gridded bed maps, a planting calendar you anchor to your own frost date, and the season log that carries this year's lessons into next year's plan.

#### FAQ

##### How do I plan a vegetable garden layout?

Measure your beds, note how many hours of sun each spot gets, sketch the beds to scale, place tall crops on the north edge, group plants by family so rotation is easy next year, and mark the paths before you place anything. One gridded page per bed keeps the whole layout visible at a glance.

##### When should I start vegetables indoors?

As a rule of thumb, most starts go 6–8 weeks before your last frost date — tomatoes and peppers at the front of that window, lettuce and brassicas closer to it. Your own frost date decides the actual week: look it up locally and count backwards on the calendar.

##### What is crop rotation and do I need it?

Rotation means not planting the same plant family in the same spot year after year — it starves the pests and soil problems that specialize in that family. The simplest rule: four groups (fruiting, roots, leafy, legumes) and each bed moves one step along that order each year. Small gardens benefit too.

##### Is a paper or app garden planner better?

By criteria: apps win reminders and automatic frost dates; paper wins visibility and durability — the map hangs where you garden, takes pencil notes in the dirt-era moments, and never needs a battery. Many gardeners run paper for the plan and log, and their phone for timer-level reminders.

[See The Vegetable Garden Planner →](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/vegetable-garden-planner.html?utm_source=fixshelf-hub&utm_medium=guide&utm_campaign=vegetable-garden-planner-printable)

### How to Reset a Messed Up Sleep Schedule (Honest Timeline + Method)

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/sleep-schedule-reset.html


Last updated: November 12, 2026

Your sleep slid to 3am and the mornings are wrecked, and the internet keeps promising fixes "in one day." Here's the honest version: how fast you recover depends on how far you drifted, the method is the same either way, and one bad night doesn't undo the work. Plain line first — this is routine-building, not medical advice; if you suspect a sleep disorder, see a doctor.

#### Why sleep schedules drift

Your body clock sets itself from cues: light, food timing, activity, and when you usually dim down. Late screens, late meals, sleeping in on weekends and doing everything under indoor light after dark all feed it the wrong cues. The clock isn't broken — it's just been trained on a different schedule than the one you want. Re-training it is a cue problem, which is why willpower at 11pm isn't the lever.

#### The reset method

1. **Fix the wake time first.** Same wake time every day, regardless of how badly you slept. This is the anchor everything else gravitates toward; bedtime follows wake time, not the reverse.

2. **Get light in the morning.** Daylight within an hour of waking is the strongest cue your clock accepts — outdoor light beats a window.

3. **Shift bedtime in small steps.** Pull it earlier by 15–30 minutes every few days rather than trying a four-hour jump your body won't accept.

4. **No catch-up weekend sleeps.** Sleeping until noon Saturday is a message that the old schedule is still the real one — it undoes the week's work.

5. **Run the same wind-down nightly.** Same sequence, same time: the cue that tells your brain sleep is the next scene.

#### How fast can you reset it?

Honest defaults from experience, not stats: a small drift (bedtime slipped an hour or two) usually re-anchors within a few consistent days. A big drift (sleeping at dawn, waking mid-afternoon) typically takes one to two weeks of unbroken consistency — and consistency is the whole treatment. The people who fail aren't doing the steps wrong; they stop after four good nights.

#### After an all-nighter

One recovery day, done right, is usually enough: stay up to a normal local bedtime (this is the one day pushing through is the point), get morning light and a short walk, keep the wake time normal the next day, and cap any nap at 20–30 minutes before noon. Skip the 12-hour rebound sleep — it restarts the drift you just paid for.

#### When ADHD keeps you up

For a lot of ADHD brains the problem isn't the clock — it's that 11pm is the first quiet hour all day, and the brain wants to use it. The wind-down that works externalizes tomorrow: ten minutes writing out tomorrow's worries and first moves so the head isn't holding them. That's the same offload mechanic as the [ADHD weekly reset](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/printable-adhd-weekly-reset.html) — bedtime edition.

#### The 4-week reset workbook

The Sleep Reset Workbook paces this method over four weeks — one habit a week, with a two-minute morning diary that shows the re-anchoring trend and the wind-down routine ready-made. If worry is what keeps you awake at night, the [Calm Mind Bundle](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/calm-mind-bundle.html) pairs it with the anxiety and overthinking pages.

#### FAQ

##### Can you fix a sleep schedule in one day?

One day fixes one all-nighter; it doesn't fix real drift. The fastest safe path: pull an all-nighter's damage back with one normal-bedtime recovery day, and fix deeper drift with a fixed wake time plus small bedtime shifts — usually several consistent days to feel re-anchored, longer to feel automatic.

##### How long does it take to reset a sleep schedule?

As workable defaults: a one-to-two-hour drift usually re-anchors in a few consistent days; a dawn-to-afternoon drift takes one to two weeks of unbroken consistency. The single biggest predictor isn't the method — it's not skipping the weekend catch-up sleep that restarts the drift.

##### How do I reset my sleep schedule after staying up all night?

Survive the day on light, movement and at most one 20-minute early nap, then go to bed at a normal local time — not early afternoon, not 3am. Set the usual wake time for the next morning and keep it. One clean recovery day beats three of drift.

##### Why do I keep messing up my sleep schedule on weekends?

Catch-up sleep: sleeping in Saturday sends your clock the signal that the old schedule is still in force, so Sunday night feels like jet lag. The rule that holds the reset together is one wake time, every day — keep weekend wake within about an hour of weekday wake and the week stops resetting itself.

[See The Sleep Reset Workbook →](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/sleep-reset-workbook.html?utm_source=fixshelf-hub&utm_medium=guide&utm_campaign=sleep-schedule-reset)

### ADHD Task Breakdown

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/adhd-task-breakdown-sheet.html


Last updated: November 12, 2026

"Just break it into smaller tasks" is the advice ADHD brains hear most and use least — because nobody shows what "smaller" means. A task like "do taxes" broken into "gather documents, fill forms, file" is still three doors with no handles. The four-column method below defines *small* as something you can see yourself doing in the next five minutes. That bar is the whole trick.

#### Why "break it down" fails ADHD brains

Executive function is the brain's project manager — the part that starts things, holds steps in mind, and switches between them. When a task's first move is vague ("start the report"), starting requires the manager to invent a plan from nothing, and ADHD brains stall exactly there. The fix isn't motivation; it's making the first move so concrete that starting needs no planning at all — just doing the visible thing in front of you.

#### The four columns

One row per task, four columns:

1. **The task** — written the way it lives in your head ("do taxes").

2. **Smallest visible first move** — physical, observable, ≤5 minutes: "open the tax folder and put last year's return on the desk." Not "gather documents." Visible means someone watching could tell you did it.

3. **What "started" looks like** — the state that proves you began: "folder open, return on desk, pen out." This kills the ambiguity that lets a started task feel unfinished.

4. **What happens after 5 minutes** — the pre-decided fork: "keep going if it's flowing; if not, close the folder and that still counts as a win." The permission to stop is what makes starting cheap.

#### Worked example (example, not a template answer)

| Task | Smallest visible first move | "Started" looks like | After 5 minutes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Do taxes | Put last year's return on the desk | Folder open, return out, pen in hand | Keep going if flowing; if not, stop — desk setup still counts |
| Email the landlord | Type "Hi" and the subject line | Draft exists with subject filled | One sentence or close; sending tomorrow is fine |

#### The 5-minute rule, defined properly

The version that works has the fourth column. "Just do it for five minutes" fails without a defined *stop*, because an open-ended five minutes feels like a commitment to the whole task. With the fork pre-decided, starting costs five minutes and carries no obligation — which is why it works on days when nothing else does.

#### The sheet

The Procrastination Rescue is this method as a reusable sheet — the four columns pre-printed, a page of worked rows, and the follow-through pages for the tasks that started but stalled. Pairs naturally with the weekly version in the [ADHD weekly reset](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/printable-adhd-weekly-reset.html), which runs this same shrinking step across a whole week.

#### FAQ

##### How do I break down tasks with ADHD?

Make the first move visible: write the task, then define a physical first step of five minutes or less — something an observer could see you do. Then note what "started" looks like and what you'll do after five minutes. Vague steps stall ADHD brains; visible, small, pre-forked steps don't need motivation to begin.

##### What is the 5-minute rule for ADHD?

A starting tactic: commit only to five minutes of a task you're avoiding, with the stop pre-decided — after five minutes you're free to continue or quit, and quitting still counts. The pre-decided exit is what makes it work; open-ended starts feel like commitments to the whole task and get avoided.

##### Why do I procrastinate on tasks I know how to do?

Because knowing how isn't the barrier — starting is. ADHD procrastination is usually a first-move problem: the task's entry point is undefined, so beginning demands planning energy the brain won't spend. Defining a visible five-minute first move moves the effort from deciding to doing.

##### Is task breakdown the same as a to-do list?

No. A to-do list stores tasks; a breakdown converts one stuck task into a startable first move plus a definition of "started" plus an exit plan. Lists fail ADHD brains at the starting line; breakdowns are built for exactly that moment.

**Want it on paper?** Four of these pages exist as a free printable PDF — [download the free ADHD sampler (no email required)](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/free-adhd-printable-sampler.html).

[See The Procrastination Rescue →](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/procrastination-rescue.html?utm_source=fixshelf-hub&utm_medium=guide&utm_campaign=adhd-task-breakdown-sheet)

### ADHD Morning Routine

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/adhd-morning-routine-checklist.html


Last updated: November 12, 2026

ADHD mornings fail for a boring reason: they demand dozens of small decisions — what to wear, what to eat, what to do first — from a brain that's worst at decisions exactly then. The fix isn't a longer routine or more discipline. It's moving the deciding to the night before, when your brain still has the fuel for it, and making the morning a pure execution list. Two parts, five minutes tonight, and the list tomorrow morning.

#### Why ADHD mornings fall apart

Executive function — the brain's start-and-sequence system — is at its lowest right after waking, and ADHD brains run it on hard mode anyway. A morning with ten implicit decisions ("I'll figure out breakfast when I get there") is ten places to stall, sit down, and lose the thread. Mornings that work have already decided everything decidable, so the sleepy brain only has to follow arrows.

#### Tonight: the 5-minute setup

1. **Write tomorrow's first three actions** — not a to-do list, just what happens after coffee.

2. **Set out clothes** — the decision that eats the most morning energy, spent in advance.

3. **Decide breakfast now** — and put the decision where you'll meet it: bowl on the counter, oats beside it. A default breakfast ("same thing every weekday") removes the decision forever.

4. **Stage the launch pad** — keys, badge, bag, meds by the door. Everything that leaves with you, in one visible spot.

5. **Set one alarm across the room** — the one that starts the sequence.

#### Tomorrow: the time-anchored checklist

Times on the left, actions on the right, no decisions between them. Example shape (an example, adjust to your hours):

| Time | Action |
|---|---|
| 6:50 | Alarm across the room → feet on floor |
| 6:55 | Meds (already on the launch pad, next to the water glass) |
| 7:00 | Breakfast — the one you decided last night |
| 7:15 | Clothes already set out → dressed |
| 7:30 | Launch pad sweep: keys, badge, bag, lunch |
| 7:40 | Out the door |

The times are anchors, not quotas — if your out-the-door is 8:10, shift every row. The structure is the point: nothing on the list requires choosing.

#### When it falls apart anyway

It will, some mornings. The comeback rule: whatever time you actually wake, *start the list from the top and skip steps rather than reordering them* — meds, breakfast, dressed, launch pad. And one bad morning doesn't retire the system; the weekly version of this repair is in the [Sunday reset](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/printable-adhd-weekly-reset.html). If racing thoughts are what's actually breaking your wake-ups, that's usually a [sleep-drift problem](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/sleep-schedule-reset.html), not a morning problem.

#### Making it stick

Both halves of this routine — tonight's setup and tomorrow's checklist — are paper-and-pen work: any sheet works. The product this extends is the [ADHD Weekly Reset](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/adhd-weekly-reset.html), whose "set the first move" step is the weekly system this checklist is the morning half of. If your mornings are fine but your tasks never start, that's the [four-column breakdown method](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/adhd-task-breakdown-sheet.html) instead.

#### FAQ

##### How do I build a morning routine that works with ADHD?

Move the decisions to the night before: write the first three actions, set out clothes, decide breakfast, and stage everything that leaves with you by the door. Then run the morning as a time-anchored checklist with no choices in it — the sleepy brain executes arrows instead of making decisions.

##### Why do mornings feel impossible with ADHD?

Executive function — the brain's starting and sequencing system — is at its lowest right after waking, and ADHD brains run it on hard mode. A morning full of small implicit decisions is a string of stall points. Removing the decisions removes the stalls; the routine stops needing willpower.

##### Should I put my medication in my morning routine?

If you take prescribed medication, the routine-friendly move is habit pairing: place it physically at a fixed step you never skip (next to the water glass at breakfast, say) so location triggers it. Timing, dosage and whether to change anything belong to your prescriber — the routine's job is only making the existing instruction hard to forget.

##### What if I keep sleeping through my alarm?

Two fixes: one alarm across the room (the getting-up is the routine's true first step), and check the night side — a 2am bedtime makes any morning routine theoretical. That's a sleep-schedule drift, and it re-anchors with a fixed wake time before any morning checklist will stick.
