### Best ADHD Daily Planner for Adults? Five Criteria That Actually Matter

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/adhd-daily-planner-adults.html


Last updated: November 12, 2026

Most "best ADHD planner" lists are ads in disguise. Here's the honest version: there is no single best planner — there's the planner you'll still be using in March, and which one that is depends on how your brain fails at planning. Five criteria predict it. Judge any planner against these.

#### Why most planners get abandoned

The pattern is reliable: an expensive beautiful planner, two devoted weeks, then it becomes a coaster. The failure isn't discipline — it's fit. Most planners are designed for brains that will naturally open the book and write today's plan every morning. ADHD brains need the planner to actively compensate: to shrink starting, survive missed days, and demand almost nothing on bad days. A planner that assumes consistent daily initiative is designed for its own abandonment.

#### The five criteria

1. **Startability** — does today's page tell you the first move, or does it hand you a blank grid and good luck? Blank grids require planning energy on arrival; pre-structured pages spend it for you.

2. **Weekly reset** — is there a built-in moment that closes last week and sets the next, so a chaotic week doesn't silently become a chaotic life? Without it, the planner only ever accumulates.

3. **Comeback path** — what does the planner do after you miss three days? A good one says "start here"; a bad one shows you the guilt of four blank days, which is exactly what makes people quit.

4. **Cost of a missed day** — does skipping a day break the system, or cost nothing? Systems with streaks and interdependent pages punish the exact failure pattern they're sold to.

5. **Printable vs app** — apps win reminders and always-with-you; paper wins visibility (the page open on the desk all day), zero notification fatigue, and the ability to see the whole week at once. Neither wins outright — it depends on whether your phone is a tool or a trap at 9am.

#### Planner types, honestly compared

By type, not brand — brands matter less than structure:

| Type | Strong on | Weak on |
|---|---|---|
| Blank daily planners | Flexibility, no prescribed system | Startability — pure blank-grid stall risk |
| Hourly schedule planners | Time-boxing for people who like structure | One missed hour cascades; comeback path usually missing |
| Planning apps | Reminders, always in pocket, resurfacing | Notification fatigue; easy to swipe away; invisible when the phone's down |
| Structured printable systems | Pre-decided page structure, visible all day, no charge cycle | No reminders; you must supply the printer |
| Bullet journals | Fully customizable | Demands system-building energy — the exact resource ADHD brains lack |

#### What we make — honestly

Full disclosure: we don't sell a daily planner. Our structured printable is weekly, not daily — the [ADHD Weekly Reset](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/adhd-weekly-reset.html) scores well on startability (pre-decided Sunday page), weekly reset (it *is* one), and comeback path (the built-in comeback page for derailed weeks), and it has the same honest gap as any printable: **no reminders**. If you need a phone to buzz, an app serves that better and we'd rather say so. For turning a stuck daily task into a startable one, the [Procrastination Rescue](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/procrastination-rescue.html) is the companion piece.

#### FAQ

##### What makes a daily planner good for ADHD adults?

Five things: pre-structured pages (no blank-grid stall), a built-in weekly reset, an explicit comeback path for missed days, near-zero penalty for skipping a day, and a format you'll actually see during the day. A planner strong on those compensates for planning energy instead of demanding it.

##### Are paper planners or apps better for ADHD?

By criteria: apps win reminders, portability and auto-resurfacing; paper wins all-day visibility, zero notification fatigue and whole-week-at-a-glance. Choose by failure mode — if you forget because nothing reminds you, apps; if apps get swiped away and lost, paper.

##### Why do I keep abandoning planners?

Fit, not discipline: most planners assume consistent daily initiative, and they punish the missed days ADHD brains reliably have — blank-page guilt, broken streaks, no restart instruction. A planner you abandon is usually one without a comeback path, not one you failed at.

##### How do I start using a planner when I never stick with it?

Start smaller than the planner asks: one page, one anchor task per day, and a fixed weekly moment to reset rather than daily perfection. If the planner has no defined "restart after a gap" move, write one on the inside cover yourself — that single page decides whether it survives March.

### ADHD Brain Dump Template

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/adhd-brain-dump-template.html


Last updated: November 12, 2026

A brain dump is the fastest way to turn 2am mental static into a piece of paper — and it's one of the few techniques that needs no discipline, no app and no routine to work. The catch: most advice stops at "write it all down." An undifferentiated pile of 40 items is its own new anxiety. The three-zone method below ends the dump with a decision, not a pile. Paper and pen; that's the whole toolkit.

#### What a brain dump does for an ADHD brain

Working memory is the brain's scratchpad — what it holds at once — and ADHD brains run it with less headroom. Every open loop (the unpaid bill, the email you owe, the thing you meant to look up) sits in that scratchpad demanding attention, which is why the head feels loud and starting anything feels impossible. Writing items down isn't organization; it's offloading — each line on paper stops paying rent in your head. That's why a dump feels physically quieter.

#### Zone 1: The dump (5 minutes, no sorting)

Set a timer for five minutes and write *everything* in your head — tasks, worries, ideas, that thing you need to remember to buy, the awkward conversation. Rules: no sorting, no judging, no organizing. Sorting mid-dump is what makes people quit; a dump's only job is offloading. Messy handwriting, arrows, duplicates — all fine.

#### Zone 2: The sort (now / today / someday)

Go down the pile and mark each item with one of three labels:

- **Now** — it's genuinely blocking something or due within hours.

- **Today** — it should happen today or this week.

- **Someday** — real, but not this week. Onto a someday page it goes, out of your head and out of today's sight.

Most of a typical dump lands in Someday — which is the point. The head was treating forty someday-items as active emergencies; the sort corrects the accounting.

#### Zone 3: The top 3

From Now and Today, circle **three** items. Not five — three is a list a bad day can finish. Each circled item gets the same treatment as the [four-column breakdown](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/adhd-task-breakdown-sheet.html): one visible five-minute first move. The dump now ends with a decision — three startable moves — instead of a pile.

#### Use it even if you never print anything

Any paper works: one page, three zones, a timer. The value is the loop, not the stationery. When the loop runs weekly, it becomes a system: the [ADHD Weekly Reset](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/adhd-weekly-reset.html) opens with a Sunday dump, sorts into its anchor-task spread, and pre-builds the comeback for a derailed week — the same mechanics across seven days. The full method is in the [Sunday reset guide](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/printable-adhd-weekly-reset.html).

#### FAQ

##### What is a brain dump for ADHD?

Writing everything in your head onto one page — tasks, worries, ideas — in one unsorted five-minute pass, then sorting it into now / today / someday and circling a top 3. It works because ADHD working memory is overloaded: each item on paper stops consuming the headroom the brain needs to actually start things.

##### How do I do a brain dump with ADHD?

Timer for five minutes, write everything without sorting or judging, then sort the pile into three zones — now, today, someday — and circle three items, each with one visible five-minute first move. The no-sorting rule matters most: sorting mid-dump is where ADHD brain dumps usually die.

##### Is a brain dump the same as journaling?

No. Journaling processes feelings and reflections in sentences; a brain dump offloads open loops as fragments in five minutes and ends with a sorted list and a top 3. Journaling asks "how do I feel about this?" — a dump asks "what's still in my head?" Both help; they solve different problems.

### DTF Print Settings

Source: https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/dtf-print-settings-checklist.html


Last updated: November 12, 2026

The prints that waste film are almost never random — they trace back to a check nobody ran: the file that wasn't mirrored, the ink density that was set for the last film batch, the powder laid on wet ink. Here's the checklist a shop tapes to the printer. Every number below is a **starting point to verify against your own film and powder spec sheets** — your consumables override anything on the internet, including this page.

#### File checks before you print

- **Mirror the art.** DTF prints face-down onto film; unmirrored text presses on backwards. Check by flipping any text layer before export.

- **Transparency where it belongs, only where it belongs.** White at 0% opacity disappears on press and the garment shows through — knock out backgrounds, but keep intended whites as solid white ink channels.

- **Resolution at print size.** Art that looks sharp on screen but is a 40% scale-up in the RIP prints soft. Check the final placed size, not the source file.

- **Gang-up placement.** Designs too close together let the powder bridge between transfers; leave a clean gutter.

#### Printer settings that matter

**Ink density** — the setting people ask about most — is how much ink the head lays down per pass. Too low and colors wash out and whites turn translucent after pressing; too high and ink pools, drying slows, and the powder sticks where it shouldn't. It's the dial that moves when you change film batches or notice whites failing. Alongside it: print resolution per your RIP's mode, the correct color mode for your workflow, and a daily nozzle/head check strip — banding you catch on a test strip is free; banding you catch on a press is a shirt.

#### Powder and cure checks

Powder goes on **evenly, while the ink is wet** — uneven coverage reads as patchy adhesion after the first wash. The melt stage matters as much: the powder needs to flow to a smooth gel before curing, not just warm up. Cure temperature and time follow your film and powder spec sheet, and they move when you change consumable brands — write the working numbers on the machine, not in someone's memory.

#### Heat press starting points

For common DTF film and powder systems, shops typically start around **290–320°F (roughly 145–160°C) for 10–15 seconds at medium-firm pressure**, with a second 5-second post-press after peeling depending on film type. These are starting points only: run a test press on scrap, check peel and wash behavior, and let your consumables' spec sheet set the final number.

#### The 60-second preflight routine

1. Flip a text layer — mirrored? ✓

2. Check whites at print size — solid, sharp? ✓

3. Test strip — no banding? ✓

4. Ink density set for *this* film batch? ✓

5. Powder coverage even, ink wet? ✓

6. Cure numbers match the current spec sheet? ✓

7. Press temp/time/pressure set and test-pressed? ✓

Thirty seconds per run buys back the film, the shirt and the customer argument. The Affinity [DTF Preflight](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/dtf-preflight-checklist.html) script automates the file-side half of this — mirror, transparency, resolution and placement checks inside Affinity before export. Doing halftones too? The [DTF Halftone](https://rastarr.github.io/fixshelf/halftone-effect-affinity.html) script generates print-safe dot structures that survive RIP and press.

#### FAQ

##### What does ink density mean in DTF printing?

Ink density is how much ink the printer lays down per pass. Too little and prints come out washed-out with translucent whites; too much and ink pools, drying drags, and powder adheres where it shouldn't. It's the first setting to check when whites fail or colors look thin after pressing.

##### What temperature do you press DTF transfers?

Typical starting range: 290–320°F (145–160°C) for 10–15 seconds at medium-firm pressure, often with a short second press after peeling. Treat that as a starting point — your film and powder spec sheet overrides any number on the internet, so test-press and verify wash results before production.

##### Why are my DTF prints banding?

Most often: clogged nozzles or a missed head check, ink density set too low for the current film, or art scaled beyond its resolution at print size. Run a test strip first — banding caught on a strip costs seconds; caught on a pressed shirt it costs the garment.

##### Do you mirror DTF prints?

Yes — DTF prints face-down onto film, so the art must be mirrored before printing or it presses onto the garment backwards. The quick check: flip any text layer and see if it reads correctly reversed on the film's print side.

#### Can ChatGPT help with ADHD planning?

Yes — usefully, if you keep it to jobs a chatbot is actually good at. It's a decent sorting engine for the brain dump, and a decent shrinker for tasks you can't start. Prompts that genuinely work:

- **The sort:** "Here is my unsorted brain dump: [paste]. Sort these into now / today / someday. Don't delete anything and don't reword them — just sort."

- **The shrink:** "Turn each of these into a task I can start in under 5 minutes, and tell me what the very first visible action is: [paste]."

- **The comeback:** "I planned 6 things today and did 1. Pick the 2 that actually matter for tomorrow and tell me what to ignore."

Print the sampler pages as the destination for that output: the dump page holds the sorted list, the breakdown sheet holds the shrunk tasks. Paper survives the tab-switch; the chat scroll doesn't.

#### FAQ

##### Are free printable ADHD planners any good?

The good ones are narrow. A free planner works when it does one job per page — a dump page, a reset page — rather than trying to be a full life-management system across 40 sheets. Judge a free pack by whether you could print one page and use it today without reading instructions.

##### What pages should an ADHD planner have?

At minimum: a brain dump page (get it out of your head), a weekly reset page (shrink the week to one anchor per day), and a comeback page (recover from missed days without scrapping the week). A task breakdown sheet is the next addition — it turns avoided tasks into five-minute starts. Apps and fancy layouts are optional; those four jobs aren't.

##### Can I use ChatGPT to help me plan with ADHD printables?

Yes — as a sorter and a shrinker, not a planner. Have it sort your brain dump into now/today/someday, shrink big tasks into five-minute starts, or pick tomorrow's two things after a blown day. Then write the results onto the printable pages, where they stay visible instead of scrolling away.
